title: Installing a close-coupled toilet from scratch
subtitle: Connect a new close-coupled WC pan and cistern to existing soil and water supply pipework
excerpt: How to install a close-coupled toilet pan and cistern onto existing soil and cold water supply pipework. Covers positioning the pan, connecting to the soil pipe, bolting the cistern, connecting the fill valve and flush valve, and commissioning.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK plumbing trade practice for WC installations.

glossaryTerms.definition: A toilet in which the cistern sits directly on the back of the pan and the two are bolted together as a single unit. The cistern outlet connects to the pan inlet through a large rubber doughnut seal (the close-coupled seal). Most new domestic WC installations in the UK use the close-coupled form; separate high-level cisterns are rare in modern new builds.

A rubber compression collar or push-fit fitting that connects the WC pan outlet to the 110 mm soil pipe. The connector compensates for slight misalignment between the pan outlet and the soil pipe centre. Soil pipe connectors come in horizontal (for a back-outlet pan into a wall) and vertical (for a floor-outlet pan into a floor socket) configurations.

content.text: installs in two stages: the pan connects to the soil pipe and fixes to the floor, and the cistern bolts to the pan. The supply connection to the cistern fill valve is the only plumbing joint. A
bridges any misalignment between the pan outlet and the existing soil pipe.

Turn off the cold water supply to the WC cistern at the nearest isolation valve or at the mains stopcock. Flush the existing cistern to empty it, then soak up any remaining water with a cloth. Where the old cistern supply pipe will be cut, hold a cloth below the cut to catch residual water in the pipe.
Position the pan on the soil pipe

Slide the soil pipe connector onto the existing 110 mm soil pipe stub. Position the pan so its outlet aligns with the connector. The connector compresses or push-fits onto the pan outlet. Adjust the pan position until it is square to the wall, using the spirit level across the rim. Mark the floor fixing holes through the pan base in pencil.
Fix the pan to the floor

Drill the floor fixing holes (the floor bolt holes in the pan base are 8 mm diameter; use 6 mm masonry plugs in tiled or concrete floors). Fit the pan back onto the soil connector and screw down through the pan base holes with the screws supplied. Do not overtighten porcelain; snug is sufficient. If the pan rocks on an uneven floor, shim with a small plastic wedge before fixing.
Bolt the cistern to the pan

Fit the close-coupled seal (large rubber doughnut) over the flush valve outlet in the base of the cistern. Lower the cistern onto the pan, aligning the seal with the pan inlet. Insert the two long cistern bolts through the cistern base and the pan back and tighten the wing nuts below the pan until the seal is compressed and the cistern sits level. Do not overtighten.
Connect the fill valve and commission

Connect the 15 mm cold supply pipe to the bottom inlet of the fill valve using the compression nut supplied. Wrap PTFE tape on the fill valve thread. Turn the supply on slowly and check for leaks around the fill valve, the cistern bolts, and the pan-soil connector. Set the cistern water level to the marked fill line inside the cistern by adjusting the float or the fill valve adjustment screw.

attrs.symptom: Water leaks from the cistern-to-pan joint after flushing
attrs.cause: Close-coupled seal not seated correctly, or cistern bolts not evenly tightened.
attrs.fix: Empty the cistern and lift it clear of the pan. Reposition the rubber seal centred on the flush valve outlet and lower the cistern again. Tighten the bolts evenly a quarter-turn at a time.

attrs.symptom: Pan outlet misses the soil connector after fixing
attrs.cause: Offset soil connectors have a maximum adjustment range; the pan may be positioned too far from the soil pipe centre.
attrs.fix: Use a wide-angle WC connector (available up to 90-degree offset) for pans that cannot be positioned directly over the soil pipe.
